offering incentives or derisking investment opportunities. Or perhaps governments 
will coerce private investors using taxes or regulations.
There are a variety of factors each government will have to consider in making 
these decisions, not least of which are effectiveness, speed, and cost. 6 These are not 
my concerns in this paper. Rather, here I focus on democratic considerations. 
Insofar as governments want to secure a democratic green transition—or a just 
green transition for those who believe justice requires democracy—attention must 
be paid not only to which policy approach will be effective, quick, or cheap, but 
also to which policy approach preserves the power of citizens to collectively coerce 
private agents through public policy. 7 To put it differently, in this paper I argue that 
to secure a democratic green transition, the state must coerce private financial 
agents, rather than just nudging or bribing them.
My focus in this paper is on the relationship of the state to private finance. This 
is, in part, of course, because this special issue sets out to address the ins and outs 
of funding the green transformation. It is also for a much deeper reason. I will 
argue in this paper that foundational to sustaining a healthy democratic state is the 
maintenance of the state’s coercive powers. Furthermore, I argue that adopting a 
policy stance that is by and large not coercive can cause the state’s coercive powers 
to erode. 8 Private finance is an area of policy marked by a historical trend of states 
choosing not to coerce private agents—hence the contemporary dominance of der -
isking policies that are the focus of much of this special issue. 9 Consequently, while 
the arguments I present here about coercion and state power are not limited to 
finance, finance, and in particular finance in the context of the green transforma -
tion, offers a particularly interesting case study.
This paper deliberately explores the space where international political economy 
(IPE) and political theory run headlong into one another. It asks, how do the 
design and implementation of macroeconomic policy impact the sustainability of 
democracy over time? More specifically, what is the differential impact on the sus -
tainability of democracy of a state pursuing the green transition through subsidies, 
credit guiding regulations, state-built green infrastructure, or reliance on corporate 
power purchase agreements (PPAs)? The answer, I suggest, lies in the observation 
that these policy designs are differentially coercive.
Coercion is a familiar concept in the IPE literature, especially when it comes to 
coercive relationships between states. 10 Kirshner’s ( 2020) book Currency and 
Coercion detailed how big states could bully small states by using what is now 
commonly referred to as monetary sovereignty. 11 Then there is the vast literature 
on interpersonal coercion, for instance, Zimmerman ( 1981) on coercive wage 
offers.12 What is less explored in the IPE literature is an idea that is generally 
accepted in the political theory literature: Coercion is justified and necessary, even 
constitutive, of a well-functioning state. 13
While I draw on the concept of coercion throughout this paper, primarily in 
its political theoretic context in which it is understood as the basis of state 
power, it is worth noting explicitly that in most contexts, coercion has a negative 
connotation. We see coercion as the act of forcing another to do what they 
would not have otherwise done. Coercion, for most of us, most of the time, 
looks like a clear violation of liberty. Consequently, it hardly seems practical, let 
alone correct, to actively promote state coercion. This, I take it, is the intuition 
private financial agents are relying on when they decry states engaging in 
694 L. DoWney
financial repression, and it is in this light that I would understand if govern -
ments who did embrace the suggestions of the paper were not quick to describe 
them publicly as coercive. Nevertheless, it seems important to me, from the per -
spectives of both democratic theory and public policy that we recognize how 
foundational coercive power, and thus coercive policy, is to sustaining a 
well-ordered democratic state. While it might seem like coercive policies are a 
violation of individuals’ liberty, it is essential to remember that in a democratic 
state, those same policies are also the expression of the citizenry’s collective 
freedom.14
Taking this as my starting point, in what follows, I argue first that coercion is 
foundational to a well-functioning democratic state, and second that it is conse -
quently dangerous for a state to get into a pattern of non-coercive policymaking 
that fails to sustain the coercive power of the state over time. The upshot is that, 
beyond considerations of effectiveness and efficiency, states have democratic reasons 
for coercing private financial firms into supporting the green transition.
Section one of the paper starts with the observation that states require coercive 
power. I then build on this observation to suggest that a well-ordered democratic 
state must deploy coercive policy. To make this argument I utilize Scott Anderson’s 
(2017) definition of coercion. This section concludes with a short discussion of 
Brett Christopher’s (2024) recent book, arguing that policies aimed at de-risking 
decarbonization are non-coercive and as such fail to contribute to sustaining the 
coercive power foundational to a well-ordered democratic state. The second section 
looks more closely at what coercing finance to fund the green transformation 
would look like. In this section, I explore environmental developmentalism, indus -
trial policy, and credit policies before considering the challenges states might face 
in adopting coercive policies of this sort. The final section summarizes and 
concludes.
Democratic states & coercion: the importance of the baseline
Max Weber famously defined the state by appealing to its monopoly over the legit -
imate use of force (2019). He distinguished between authority based on coercion 
and authority based on a constellation of interests, defining law as an ‘order whose 
validity is externally underwritten by the Chance that physical or mental coercion 
will be applied by a specialised staff of people whose task is to enforce conformity 
or punish contravention’ (Weber, 2019, p. 112). 15 In a much more recent book, 
political philosopher Philip Pettit ( 2023) outlined the function of the modern state 
as establishing a coercive territorial regime of law that ordered the lives of its cit -
izenry.16 John Rawls ( 1999) wrote, ‘a legal system is a coercive order of public rules 
addressed to rational persons for the purpose of regulating their conduct and pro -
viding the framework for social cooperation’ (p. 235). 17
A well-ordered state, of any sort, requires some degree of coercion because 
states aim to coordinate resources, and coercion is fundamental to this. If they 
could not coerce, states would be left trying to coordinate activity by appealing to 
interests. This is one crucial difference between private and public institutions. 
Private institutions and firms generally cannot coerce. Consequently, they must 
appeal to the interests of individuals to encourage them to act as desired. In fact, 
when private firms are able to coerce individuals, whether through their power as 
RevIe W oF  InteRnA tIonAL  PoLItICAL  eConoMy 695
employers or through market power, we tend to think of their coercive actions as 
illegitimate.18
As Lowi ( 1972, p. 299) put it in the epigraph to this paper, ‘the most significant 
fact about government is that government coerces’ . 19 That being the case, we can 
say that the most significant fact about democratic government is that citizens col -
lectively wield the state’s powers of coercion. 20 The state, as Klein ( 2022) wrote, is 
the ‘infrastructure of power through which the people can act’ (2022, p.37). 21 
Under a democratic system of government, citizens guide the state collectively and 
are coerced by state power individually, with the latter being a condition of the 
former.22 While a democratic state may require that the state’s coercive powers be 
wielded in a particular way, it is nevertheless still the case that a democratic state 
requires the sustained power to coerce its citizens. Consequently, sustaining a 
healthy democratic state throughout the green transformation will require, among 
other things, the maintenance of that state’s coercive powers. 23
Democratic states deploy their coercive force through the design, implementa -
tion, and enforcement of public policy. When the state makes and enforces coercive 
public policy it does two things. First, it forces citizens to act in ways they may 
not have otherwise done. Second, it sustains and bolsters the power of the state 
over its citizens. Different scholars see each of these as paradigmatic of coercion. 
Robert Nozick transformed the literature on coercion with an essay he wrote in 
1969.24 Central to Nozick’s conception of coercion is the distinction between offers 
and threats.25 For him, broadly, threats are coercive and offers are not. The distinc -
tion between the two rests on the concept of a baseline (Nozick, 1969, p. 447). 26 A 
threat changes the baseline state of affairs that the coercee faces, whereas an offer 
does not. 27 If I hold a gun to your head and say, ‘your shoes or I’ll shoot you’ , I 
have changed the baseline. Prior to my utterance, your baseline state of affairs 
included possessing your shoes and did not include being shot. After my utterance, 
that changed. The expectation is that you will be shot unless you act in accordance 
with my wishes. By contrast, suppose I say, if you give me your shoes now, I’ll buy 
you two new pairs tomorrow. Y our baseline state of affairs—being alive and having 
your shoes—hasn’t changed. In sum, Nozick’s view of coercion centers on the idea 
that to coerce is to force someone else to act as they otherwise would not have done.
Scott Anderson ( 2017) described coercion in a different way. For him, the key 
element of coercion was not the threat or the shifting baseline, but rather, the 
coercer’s accumulation of power.28 For Anderson, coercion was ‘any kind of activity 
by a powerful agent who creates and then utilises a significant disparity in power 
over another in order to constrain or alter the latter’s possibilities for action’ ( 2017, 
p. 1). 29 In contrast to Nozick, coercion in Anderson’s view is not merely about 
pressuring someone into making a particular decision. Rather, for Anderson, the 
essential core of coercion is the power differential that enables an agent to exert 
such pressure successfully. Consequently, if as I observed above, a well-ordered 
democratic state requires coercive power, then in Anderson’s view, establishing and 
sustaining just such a state requires coercive policy.
Coercive policy
A state that progressively taxes wealth not invested in assets compatible with the 
green transformation is engaging in coercive policy in both Anderson and Nozick’s 
696 L. DoWney
(1969) view. According to Nozick, it is coercive because it eliminates the status quo 
as an option. Wealthy individuals can no longer invest in the same way without 
being subject to penalizing taxes. According to Anderson, it is coercive because the 
state ‘intentionally accumulates the power needed to constrain others broadly (say, 
by arming herself), and then employs or threatens to employ such powers in this 
way’ (2017, p. 12). 30
In Anderson’s view, coercive policies would be those through which the state 
accumulates and exercises the power to ‘constrain or alter’ citizens’ ‘possibilities for 
action’ (2017, p.1).31 Nudge policies, by contrast, are those that suggest to citizens 
that they should do something differently, or perhaps they make the desired action 
easier or more convenient to achieve. 32 Climate disclosure policies are a great 
example. They aim to make green investment more likely by giving private inves -
tors more relevant information, however, in so doing they do not substantially bol -
ster the power of the state over investors.
Policies that work through attraction are similar to nudge policies in shape but 
stronger in pull. They influence individual behaviour by making particular actions 
more attractive. A clear example of attraction policies are subsidies. When states 
deploy subsidies to make the production and purchase of electric vehicles (EVs) 
more attractive, they are deploying attraction policies. When states deploy fixed 
input tariffs with the intention of making renewable energy projects bankable, they 
are deploying attraction policies. 33
In Anderson’s (2017) view, attraction policies are clearly noncoercive. 34 Suppose 
a state wants to increase investment in battery technology. It has two options: Offer 
private investors inducements to make the relevant investments more desirable, or 
require them to make the relevant investments. 35 Both options work by altering the 
option set the private investors face, the former by making the desired option more 
attractive, the latter by a requiring particular action and thereby eliminating the 
status quo as an option. 36 What makes one approach coercive and the other not, 
in Anderson’s ( 2017) view, is the difference in the power dynamic each policy 
approach produces. In the former case, the private investors get the upper hand. 
Subsidies influence agents’ actions by appealing to their existing interests. By con -
trast, in the latter case, the state intentionally deploys its power to constrain the 
actions of private investors. 37
Anderson’s (2017) view, in focusing on the power dynamic between the would-be 
coercer and coercee, enables us to capture more complicated policy arrangements 
as well. Contrary to Nozick’s ( 1969) sharp distinction between offers and threats, 
philosophers now recognize the possibility that some offers can be coercive. They 
call these throffers (threat + offer). Suppose, for instance, that the state offers utility 
companies subsidies to support their transition to renewable energies but further 
stipulates that regardless of whether the company accepts the offer, regulations will 
soon require that companies make the transition. It is like me saying, ‘sell me your 
shoes at the top price, or I’ll shoot you’ . The United States’ (US) approach to EVs 
is a compelling example. The government has announced a wide variety of policies 
in the form of offers to incentivize companies to make EVs and consumers buy 
them, including production credits, manufacturing conversion grants, loans to 
domestic manufacturers, tax credits for purchases, and more. These policies are 
meant to encourage the desired outcome—a transition to EVs. These offers have 
now been followed up with a regulatory proposal that would require car companies 
RevIe W oF  InteRnA tIonAL  PoLItICAL  eConoMy 697
to meet much higher efficiency standards, in effect requiring that they produce 
EVs. Taken as a policy package, this looks very much like a throffer. 38 Furthermore, 
even if it makes the transition easier through the use of subsidies, such a policy 
package does ultimately exercise and bolster the power of the state to limit the 
choice set of private financial agents. As such, in Anderson’s ( 2017) view, it is 
coercive.
Should states decide to embrace the use of coercive policies in funding a green 
transition, it is likely that those coercive policies will take the form of throffers—a 
sweetened form of coercion. As I argue in the next section, derisking is a 
non-coercive approach to guiding finance. Over time, the state’s reliance on this 
approach has eroded the state’s power and bolstered that of private finance. As 
such, any attempt to embrace coercive policy today will need to be sweetened, as 
the state will be attempting to coerce very powerful private agents without much 
capacity of their own. 39
De-risking as non-coercive
Policies that aim to attract or bribe private finance into supporting green (or oth -
erwise state desired) investments are what many in the literature, including this 
special issue, have called ‘de-risking’ policies (see Gabor & Braun, this issue; Gabor, 
2020, 2021; Kedward et  al., 2022, 2024; Christophers, 2024).40 Far from the state 
coercing private finance, if anything, derisking decarbonization looks more like pri -
vate financial agents coercing the state. Their aims are very clear—investments that 
will generate relatively risk-free returns—and their threat is credible—to take their 
money elsewhere. 41 If states rely on derisking policies, private financial agents are 
empowered to determine the terms of conditions of the transition. This can pro -
duce a ratchet effect, or a hostage situation, in which the only way that the state 
can achieve its desired aim is by meeting the increasing demands of private finan -
cial agents.
In his recent book, The Price is Wrong , Brett Christophers ( 2024) described just 
such a process when it comes to state subsidies on renewable electricity genera -
tion.42 In an effort to get the private sector to invest in and produce green energy 
states aim to make related investments attractive either through subsidies, implicit 
or explicit, or guarantees like those secured through a fixed input tariff. 43 
Christophers ( 2024) observed that once such a system was in place it was nearly 
impossible to remove without causing a collapse in renewable energy generation as 
it was the state subsidy or guarantee that made the projects bankable in the first 
place, and the underlying economics of electricity generation made this unlikely to 
change (p. 297). 44
Most important for our purposes is the observation that this arrangement puts 
the private financial agents in the driver’s seat when it comes to achieving the 
public aim of the green transition (Christophers, 2024, p. 257). 45 Through these 
derisking arrangements, private financial agents accumulate power over states, 
rather than the other way around. They are empowered to say, ‘if you take away 
our subsidies, we’ll stop producing renewable energy’ , or in some cases, ‘if you 
don’t increase your support, we’ll stop’ .
In Vietnam, for instance, the year after the state support in the form of feed-in 
tariffs ended ‘solar installations collapsed—literally, to zero’ (Christophers, 2024, 
698 L. DoWney
296).46 Developers have argued that private ‘power-purchase-agreement terms are 
‘unbankable’ without curtailment guarantees’ from state owned enterprises (SOEs) 
and state guarantees on those payments (Larsen, this issue, 9). In other words, if 
the state does not intervene to make these investments more appealing, the money 
will not be forthcoming. Christophers ( 2024) argued that this was clear evidence 
of the fact that the fundamentals of this market required ongoing support. I simply 
observe that it is also evidence of the power private financial agents hold over the 
state when it comes to securing the investments integral to decarbonization, and 
that this power is, in part, a product of the state’s use of attraction-policies.
One could challenge this claim by observing that even in such a situation, the 
state retains the formal power to act however it pleases. In other words, in what 
way exactly does a pattern of derisking erode the power of the state to coerce over 
time? Why would deploying a pattern of non-coercive policy over time, make it 
harder for the state to coerce in the future? The answer is partly informal, in that 
over time, when a state doesn’t coerce private finance, state actors—policymakers, 
legislators, and even citizens—begin to believe that they cannot, or that it is too 
difficult or too expensive to do so. Their imagination about what is possible 
through policy, and their expectations about what will or will not happen adapt to 
the given policy pattern (Downey, 2021).47
A pattern of derisking will also, over time, influence the formal power relation -
ship between private finance and the state. Derisking works by making investments 
more appealing to private financial agents. A pattern of derisking policy conse -
quently results in private financial agents profiting as well as engaging in more of 
the desired set of investments, be those green energy companies, relevant infra -
structure, or basic technology companies. The consequence is that the relevant pri -
vate financial agents, through a pattern of derisking policies, grow their wealth and 
gain in experience, knowledge, and ownership of the physical infrastructure and 
core technologies central to the green transition. Over time, then, the opportunity 
cost of those financial agents disengaging or leaving becomes higher and higher. 
They gain power over the state.
Some scholars have argued that an approach to securing the green transition 
that relies on de-risking policies that aim to attract or bribe private finance will 
simply not be effective (see Christophers, 2024).48 Others have observed that rely -
ing on the private sector in this way means that the state does not develop the 
requisite capacity in the form of expertise, personnel, and infrastructure (Blyth & 
Driscoll, this issue). 49 I have argued here that securing the green transition through 
de-risking alone erodes state power because it is fundamentally non-coercive. 
Rather than the state designing, implementing, and enforcing policy such that 
power accumulates in the state to force citizens, most especially private financial 
agents, to act in particular ways, it does the opposite, allowing private financial 
agents to accumulate power they can use to steer public policy.
Coercing decarbonization
Perhaps the most well-known example of states deploying coercive policies to shape 
the macroeconomic environment is what is commonly referred to as the develop -
mental state (Johnson, 1982; Thurbon, 2014).50 As Kim and Thurbon described it:
RevIe W oF  InteRnA tIonAL  PoLItICAL  eConoMy 699
Developmentalism embodies an inherently political view of the economy; in the eyes of 
policymakers, the purpose of economic activity is to promote national security and prestige 
in what is perceived to be an inherently competitive and hostile international arena. The 
goal of industrial governance is therefore to promote local manufacturing capacity, techno -
logical autonomy and export competitiveness for nation-building and nation-sustaining 
purposes. For this reason, amongst the policymaking elite, the practice of strategically 
intervening in the economy in pursuit of these goals is accepted as both necessary and 
desirable. (2015, p. 216) 51
The powers of developmentalism have recently been tuned to address the cli -
mate crisis more directly. Robert MacNeil ( 2017) has argued that this shift is not 
necessarily straightforward as the developmental state model is better suited to 
facilitating a shift towards particular sectors, rather than away from others. As he 
put it, in the case of the green transition, ‘the state is required to purposefully 
undermine and destroy conventional energy’ (MacNeil, 2017, p. 51). 52 While this 
has required a shift in the structures of many developmental states, MacNeil argued 
that it had proven especially hard in the context of ‘hidden’ developmental states 
like that found in the U.S. (Block 2008).
By contrast, Thurbon et  al. ( 2023) documented in great detail a system that they 
referred to as environmental developmentalism in which states in East Asia 
deployed state power to support green investment and to reduce investment in 
dirty and polluting sectors. 53 The creative destruction approach that they outlined 
was a mixed approach to state intervention that entailed offers, threats, and throf -
fers. In the case of Korea, the environmental developmentalism approach entailed 
direct public investments, approximately 2% of GDP between 2009 and 2013, 
alongside coercive regulations (Kim & Thurbon, 2015; Thurbon et  al., 2023).54 For 
instance, in 2012, the government mandated that the state’s largest utility compa -
nies generate 4% of their energy from renewables by 2015 and 10% by 2022 (Kim 
& Thurbon, 2015; MacNeil, 2017).55
Essential to the Korean case, according to Kim and Thurbon ( 2015), was the 
presence of a preexisting developmental state approach to economic policy. Key to 
the emergence of developmental environmentalism were long standing institutions 
aimed at ‘strategically intervening in the economy in pursuit of ’ goals such as 
‘national security and prestige’(Kim & Thurbon, 2015).56 Previously, the Korean 
developmental state had achieved economic success through the use of a develop -
mental state model which deployed a range of coercive policies and relied heavily 
on fossil fuels. ‘Between 1990 and 2007, Korea’s carbon emissions grew the fastest 
in the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), making 
it the world’s ninth largest CO 2 emitter’(Kim & Thurbon, 2015, p. 214). 57
Kim and Thurbon ( 2015) argued that the shift in Korea from developmentalism 
to developmental environmentalism was a change in the perspective of policy elites 
as to what served their developmental aims. In other words, in the Korean case, 
the coercive tools and the state’s willingness to use them had long been present. 
What changed was the state’s aim, with the emergence of green growth as a moti -
vating target.
While developmentalism, and now environmental developmentalism, is generally 
associated with East Asian states, western nations are increasingly embracing what 
Aiginger and Rodrik ( 2020), as well as Chang and Andreoni ( 2020), have separately 
referred to as ‘industrial policy in the twenty-first century’ . 58 Aiginger and 
Rodrik wrote:
700 L. DoWney
Summarizing, industrial policy is a systemic approach that coordinates [sic] innovation, 
regional policy, and trade policy…It should be steered by societal goals…Extending far 
beyond the correction of market failures, it is a search process in the unknown that not 
only profits from a dialog with experts, interest groups, and citizens but must also avoid 
hijacking by special interest groups and populism. (2020, p. 203) 59
The first thing to note is that this sort of industrial policy moves beyond fixing 
market failures, and instead, seeks clearly articulated substantive policy aims. 60 
Kathleen McNamara ( 2024) described this in the contemporary European context 
as ‘visibly interventionist European industrial policy and geopolitical market strat -
egy’ that explicitly picked winners and losers. 61 Mazzucato and Rodrik ( 2023) have 
developed a taxonomy of industrial policies that include what they called ‘condi -
tionalities’ .62 In this way, many of the industrial policies we see emerging today 
contrast with what scholars have previously referred to as the hidden developmen -
tal state, an approach to macroeconomic which dominated U.S. policy since the 
1980s. Under the hidden developmental state, the policy was intentionally 
non-coercive (Block 2008; Block et  al., 2024; MacNeil, 2017; Popp Berman, 2022).63
States are increasingly embracing an approach to economic policy—industrial 
policy or developmental environmentalism—that embraces state intervention, direc -
tion, and direct action (Alami & Dixon, 2024; Petry et  al., 2023; Schindler et  al., 
2023;).64 As part of this shift, there are plenty of climate-related policies that are 
coercive: Requirements for companies to reduce emissions, carbon taxes, bans on 
fossil fuel-based cars, and so on. What is less common, and what I have advocated 
for in this paper, is state coercion of private finance in pursuit of the green 
transition.
Credit policy
Brett Christophers ( 2024) has argued that critiques of de-risking are ‘not particu -
larly helpful’ . ‘Unless the state’ , he wrote, ‘were willing and able widely to compel 
private sector actors to invest in the development of such [renewable energy] infra -
structure against their own volition, it is hard to see what good would come of a 
refusal to de-risk’(Christophers, 2024, p. 351). 65 Christophers is arguing here from 
the perspective of efficacy. In other words, de-risking is likely an essential policy 
tool if we are to achieve the green transition at all. What I have argued in this 
paper is that, while Christophers may be right about this, it is also true that for 
such a transition to be democratic it will require that the state does not only attract 
and nudge but also coerces private finance. One obvious opportunity for doing just 
that is through credit policy.
At the tail end of the first Trump Presidency, the Office for the Comptroller of 
the Currency (OCC)—one of the primary bank regulators in the US—proposed a 
regulatory rule which aimed to prevent banks from lending based on criteria other 
than pre-determined quantitative profit calculations (2021). In other words, it 
would prohibit banks making credit allocation decisions based on things like 
Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) standards. Implicit in this rule is the 
idea that the state, in the form of the OCC in this instance, should decide what 
are the reasonable bases for credit allocation. Under Trump, the OCC suggested 
that the only reasonable basis was quantitative profit calculations ( 2021).66 It is 
entirely reasonable to suppose, however, that the state might decide that securing 
RevIe W oF  InteRnA tIonAL  PoLItICAL  eConoMy 701
the green transformation is a policy priority. Credit guidance is one form of coer -
cive policy that could help achieve that. Instead of requiring that banks, and other 
credit providers, make investment decisions based on pre-determined profit calcu -
lations, they might require a particular investment pattern more in line with decar -
bonization. This is not a new idea.
Historically, credit policy was seen as the third leg of macroeconomic policy, 
alongside monetary and fiscal policy (see Douglas et  al., 1950; Monnet, 2018, 
2023).67 The aim of credit policy was to steer investment—public and private—
through the state provision of credit, but also through the regulation of private 
investment. There are at least two ways in which modern states could deploy coer -
cive credit policy in pursuit of the green transition. The first is for the state to 
require private financial agents to make the desired investments. The second is for 
the state to make the investments itself. Both are coercive in the sense that both 
exert and bolster the power of the state to alter and limit the choices set citizens 
face (Dikau & Volz, 2023; Geiger, 2008; van’t Klooster & van Tilburg, 2020).68
States could require private financial agents to make the desired investments in 
a few ways. 69 The first is to change the requirements financial agents face when 
interacting with the state. The most obvious example of this is collateral require -
ments. When private financial agents come to the state for liquidity support, they 
have to post collateral. Collateral requirements could be made to incorporate green 
assets. Second, some states require banks to lend a certain percentage of their 
assets to priority sectors, including renewable energy. The Reserve Bank of India, 
for instance, requires that 40% of all bank loans go to priority sectors, which now 
include renewable energies. 70 Other states mandate interest rate discounts for pri -
ority sectors. Such policies bolster the power of the state over private financial 
agents by forcing them to comply with green investment requirements. Third, states 
could regulate against investment in particular assets in the form of lending limits 
or exclusions. 71
States could also make the desired investments themselves (Christophers, 2024).72 
This is perhaps the most familiar form of coercive credit policy but that which we 
are least likely to intuitively categorize as coercive. It includes direct state invest -
ment in relevant research and development, state engagement in infrastructure and 
production, as well as the use of state investment banks and other SOEs to do the 
same. Examples of this approach are endless. They include everything from the 
Korean state directly investing in green research and development to green invest -
ments made by state investment banks (see Aiginger & Rodrik, 2020; Kedward 
et  al., 2022; Macfarlane & Mazzucato, 2018; MacNeil, 2017; Mazzucato, 2022).73 
Such state action might not, at first, seem coercive, as it does not have the intuitive 
feel of forcing someone to act in a particular way. After all, the state is engaging 
in the investment itself, in what way is it coercing others?
To see why direct state investment is coercive in the relevant sense we must go 
back to the definition of coercion. Both dominant definitions of coercion—Nozick’s 
Nozick ( 1969) and Anderson’s ( 2017)—are situated in time. For Nozick, this is 
most obvious as his definition requires the identification of a baseline that is in 
place before the coercive action occurs (1969). For Anderson, the same is true in 
the form of what we might call a baseline balance of power (2017). An action is 
coercive, relative to this baseline, if it creates and utilizes a disparity in power in 
order to change the coercee’s possibilities for action. In other words, coercing, 
702 L. DoWney
bolsters the coercer’s balance of power over the coercee. If the baseline state of 
affairs is a state without income tax, then imposing income tax is, by this view, 
coercive (Nozick, 1969, pp. 169-172). 74 This seems counterintuitive to most readers 
because the baseline is so distant, but it is consistent with the definition. What I 
have suggested here is that, against a baseline of non-coercive derisking policies, 
engaging in direct state investment is coercive, because it tilts the balance of power 
between the state and private finance in favour of the state by exercising the state’s 
power to change citizens’ ‘possibilities for action’ (Anderson, 2017, p. 1). 75
All forms of credit policy require that the state take an explicit stance on what 
constitutes a priority asset—what it wants to see more investment in, and what less. 
In order to coerce private finance, the state must first articulate what it wants pri -
vate financial agents to do. That means the development of a classification of assets, 
which would require political engagement and state capacity (Mazzucato, 2022).76 
While definitely difficult, and a shift away from the norm of avoiding explicitly 
choosing winners and losers, this is far from impossible.
During World War I, the Fed established the Capital Issues Committee (CIC) to 
‘prevent a diversion of capital into industries not essential to the war effort’ (Dill, 
1971).77 To that end, the committee examined all prospective stocks and bonds 
worth more than US$100,000 to determine which served ‘the national interest’ and 
which did not. The CIC could not prevent private issuance of stocks and bonds, 
but its public disapproval did have serious negative impacts on marketability.
Eric Monnet has written extensively on the French use of credit policy in the 
post-war period (2018). 78 He has concluded that ‘the correlation between high 
growth and financial restraints in post-war Europe is a robust fact’ (Monnet, 2018, 
p. 211). 79 To this end, Monnet has subsequently proposed establishing an indepen -
dent European credit council (2023; Feldmann, 2024).80 Monnet writes ‘a European 
Credit Council at the European level would coordinate the various policy actions 
of the European Union to ensure the financing of its general objectives’ (2023, p. 
21).81 Monnet’s credit council would not follow the CIC in offering (or denying) 
state approval of particular assets. Much more modestly, the council would offer 
the European Parliament (EP) the expertise required to challenge, monitor, and 
sometimes compliment the credit policy implicitly conducted by the European 
Central Bank (ECB).
The EP itself has already established a taxonomy of sustainable assets. To be a 
sustainable asset, according to the European Union (EU)’s taxonomy, assets must 
substantially contribute to at least one of a set of stated objectives and do no sig -
nificant harm to any others. Furthermore, the EU has required that sustainable 
assets meet some set of minimum social standards, above and beyond the ‘green’ 
objectives. While the taxonomy is not without its detractors, in a basic sense, the 
EU has outlined a mechanism for identifying preferred assets (Kedward et  al., 
2024).82
Non-coercive policies have long dominated macroeconomic policy (Braun & 
Gabor, this issue; Kedward et  al., 2022).83 This has led to the development of pow -
erful private agents, a diminished state reputation, and eroded state capacity. 
Consequently, when governments are faced with the question, of what sorts of pol -
icies should deploy to finance the green transition, they are presented with this 
question in the context of depleted state capacity, a point that Blyth and Driscoll 
compellingly defend in this issue. That makes securing a democratic approach to 
RevIe W oF  InteRnA tIonAL  PoLItICAL  eConoMy 703
the transition even more difficult. It requires both (1) deploying depleted state 
powers of coercion to coerce private finance, and (2) simultaneously building the 
state’s capacity to coerce.
The first is particularly difficult in the context of a globalized financial system. 
A weakened state that attempts to coerce private financial agents into complying 
with its stated political aims will clearly run the risk of walking away. In other 
words, attempting to democratically steer investment could cause a state to lose 
investment. There are two responses to this challenge. The first is to observe that 
this is an equilibrium problem. Private investors may choose to leave a particular 
political jurisdiction in the face of coercive policies if there are other, more attrac -
tive political jurisdictions to which they can move. Consequently, when most states 
are relying on a pattern of non-coercive policy to finance the green transition, it is 
more difficult to deploy coercive policies. By contrast, as more states embrace the 
coercive approach, private investors have fewer regulatory havens to which they 
can flee.
The second is a policy response: Capital controls. These are coercive policies 
that make it much more difficult for private finance to up sticks and leave if they 
don’t like the policies in a given state. As Eric Helleiner pointed out in discussing 
the Bretton Woods period, capital controls have long been recognized as a coercive 
form of policy that bolsters state power:
The bankers were also concerned about the compatibility of capital controls with a liberal 
democratic form of government. Whereas Keynes and White had viewed controls on the 
investment behavior of a wealthy minority as essential for a government’s political auton -
omy, their critics viewed such controls as overly ‘coercive’ and reminiscent of the ‘Hitlerian 
monetary system’ . (Helleiner, 2015, p. 41) 84
More recently, scholars have argued in favour of ‘imposing coercive limits on 
cross-border capital mobility’ by appealing to global justice considerations (Cordelli 
& Levy, 2022).85
Finally, it is worth observing that not all states are the same. Some states are 
particularly attractive places for private financial actors to reside and to invest. 
Those more desirable jurisdictions may find that they could more easily embrace 
coercive policies, as it would take more to cause private financial agents to leave. 
This is evidenced clearly by the concept of hot money as it relates to developing 
nations. Private finance is more readily prepared to pick up and leave developing 
countries. By contrast, it would take a lot for a big bank to decide to leave the US.
Combining these observations offers one conclusion. To create the conditions 
for securing a democratic green transition, we must see movement away from the 
existing macroeconomic policy equilibrium in which the non-coercive policy 
framework prevails. The only way out of that particular equilibrium is for those 
jurisdictions where private finance currently prefers to reside to act first.
Alternatively, one might conclude that relying on state governments to solve this 
problem independently, regardless of who moves first, is untenable and instead a 
systemic approach to this problem is required. Others in this special issue make 
exactly this argument (van’t Klooster & van Tilburg, 2020; van’t Klooster and 
Prodani, this issue). 86 The difficulty with such an approach is that it faces power 
imbalance issues: Some states hold coercive power over others. The obstacle to 
such a systemic, non-statist approach to the problem it seems, is the simple 
704 L. DoWney
observation that, as things currently stand, there is no presumption of political 
equality between states. Consequently, it is hard to imagine those states which hold 
coercive power over others embracing a systemic solution to the problem which 
does not itself bolster and sustain their own coercive powers.
Summary and conclusion
States are foundationally coercive entities. That is, in part, what makes them states. 
Their entire aim is to alter the choice set of citizens, to coordinate actions and 
resources. This is just as true of democratic states as it is of any others. In fact, 
the coercive power of the state is the mechanism through which citizens are able 
to engage in self-government. The coercive power of the state gives effect to the 
democratic will. Consequently, to secure a green transformation that does not 
erode democracy requires a policy approach that preserves the coercive power of 
the state.
Following Anderson, I adopted the view that coercive acts are those which 
intentionally accumulate ‘the power needed to constrain others broadly’ and then 
employ or threaten ‘to employ such power in this way’ (Anderson, 2017, p. 12). 87 
Utilizing this conception of coercion, I outlined coercive policies as those which 
bolster and exercise the power of the state to limit or shape citizens’ decision sets. 
I contrasted coercive policies with nudge and attraction policies, the classic exam -
ple of which is a subsidy. These sorts of non-coercive policies induce agents to act 
in the desired way by making it more appealing based on their existing preferences. 
Derisking, as a ‘form of conservative worldmaking by and for finance’ , fits this 
mould perfectly (Eich, this issue). 88
I then argued that the problem with a policy strategy that relies on derisking 
green investment is that it fails to coerce, and in so doing, fails to sustain the 
coercive power of the state over private financial agents. Consequently, to secure a 
green transformation that sustains democracy, the state must coerce private finance, 
even if it does so alongside de-risking offers, inducements, and guarantees. 89 In the 
second section of the paper, I outline in more detail some of the ways states might 
coerce private financial agents through the use of credit policy.
This paper brings together the concept of coercive state power from political 
theory with discussions of policy design and decarbonization in IPE using the sim -
ple observation that the form macroeconomic policy takes, over time, influences 
the sustainability and strength of democracy. In other words, the difference between 
the tax subsidies offered in the Inflation Reduction Act to promote EVs production 
and consumption, credit regulations that require banks and shadow banks to invest

summary_html:
Main argument: Leah Downey argues that securing a democratic green transition requires the state to actively coerce private financial agents to fund decarbonization efforts rather than merely nudging or incentivizing them. This coercion is essential to maintain the state’s foundational democratic power and capacity over time, preventing private finance from gaining undue influence over public policy.

Research design: The paper uses a conceptual and normative approach, engaging political theory on coercion alongside international political economy discussions on macroeconomic policy and finance for decarbonization. It contrasts coercive and non-coercive policy approaches, analyzing their implications for democratic state power.

Method: Analytical and theoretical, synthesizing political theory definitions of coercion (notably from Scott Anderson and Robert Nozick) with empirical and case-based illustrations such as developmental state models and macro-financial policies related to green transitions.

Dataset or evidence: The paper draws on secondary research and literature, including policy case studies from South Korea’s environmental developmentalism, U.S. inflation reduction policies, regulatory proposals on credit allocation, and critiques of derisking financial policies. It cites recent books, government regulations, and comparative political economy scholarship.

Unit of analysis: The main unit is the democratic state’s use of coercive versus non-coercive macroeconomic policies to shape private financial actors’ investment decisions in the context of funding the green transition.

Time period studied: Primarily contemporary and recent historical periods, focusing on developments in the 21st century, with reference to historical cases such as post-war credit policy and recent policy shifts up to 2025.

Geographic focus: The analysis highlights cases from the United States, South Korea, the European Union, Vietnam, and general East Asia, with attention to the global financial system’s impact on policy choice and state capacity.

Identification strategy: The argument is developed through theoretical reasoning and illustrative case examples rather than formal causal inference or quantitative analysis. The paper identifies coercion by contrasting policy approaches that alter baseline power relations between states and private finance.

Key findings: - Sustained democratic governance depends on maintaining the state’s coercive power over private finance, which non-coercive derisking policies undermine. - Non-coercive policies like subsidies and derisking empower private finance, enabling them to influence or block public green transition goals. - Coercive policies—such as credit guidance, regulatory mandates, taxation, and direct state investment—are necessary to restore state capacity and steer private finance toward decarbonization. - Policy mixes involving “throffers” (combined threats and offers) are practical ways states can coerce while retaining some incentives. - The global financial system constrains states’ willingness and ability to coerce due to capital mobility, but coordinated action or capital controls may mitigate this. - Environmental developmentalism in East Asia exemplifies successful coercive intervention for green industrial policy, showing the state’s pivotal role in directing the transition. - The green finance gap will not close without a democratic, coercive state strategy that rejects over-reliance on the financial sector’s voluntarism.

Main limitations: The paper does not empirically test its claims with quantitative or primary data, relying on conceptual arguments and selective qualitative examples. It assumes democratic states can build coercive capacity despite global capital constraints, a prospect that may be optimistic. The normative stance on coercion may be contested, and practical political obstacles to implementing coercive policies are acknowledged but not empirically explored in depth.

Why this matters for IR scholars: This paper bridges democratic political theory and international political economy, highlighting how macrofinancial policy design shapes state power and democracy in the green transition. It underscores the importance of state capacity and coercion in global decarbonization governance debates, cautioning against insufficient attention to power dynamics between states and private finance. It advances understanding of how state strategies affect international cooperation and competition over climate finance and technological sovereignty.

Why this matters for strategic infrastructure research: The argument centers directly on the geopolitical and political-economic significance of energy infrastructure financing and the strategic role of state coercive power. It illuminates the risks of private financial dominance over critical green infrastructure and technology investments, making a case that democratic states must harness coercive macrofinancial tools (including credit policy and capital controls) to ensure secure, sovereign, and just energy transitions. This insight is vital for scholars and policymakers focused on great power competition, industrial policy, and the governance of AI and emerging technologies linked to climate infrastructure.

title: Digital Tuvalu: state sovereignty in a world of climate loss
abstract: Abstract In a widely shared video, the government of the island state of Tuvalu posed an imaginary of Tuvalu as a digital nation in a situation of unabated climate change. In this article, we take the example of Digital Tuvalu as a paradigmatic case to advance the debates on international relations in the Anthropocene, demonstrating how the processes of climate catastrophe and digital state formation juxtapose. In linking climate loss and state extinction to notions of virtual sovereignty and cyber statehood, we are attentive to the infrastructural power of large information and communications technology companies, while at the same time acknowledging the agency of the Tuvaluan state in navigating the challenges of the Anthropocene. We discuss how a virtual deterritorial state mobilizes the Tuvaluan indigenous philosophy of fenua, to link land, sea, people and culture in a relational understanding of territory and sovereignty. Digital Tuvalu in this way envisions emerging digital technologies to rebuild Tuvaluan fenua in virtual space, thereby regaining agency in the face of existential climate threats. This, we argue, signals a new and highly relational model of digital state preservation, having profound implications for international relations in the Anthropocene.

An island state existing purely in the metaverse; such was the image of a possible 
future that went viral after the video release by Tuvalu’s government of a new 
programme entitled Te Ataeao Nei (known in English as Future Now).1 The video 
was launched by Simon Kofe, then minister for justice, communication and 
foreign affairs,2 at COP27, the UN climate conference (Conference of the Parties 
of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change) held in November 2022 
in Sharm-El-Sheikh, Egypt. 3  At the beginning of the recording, Kofe appears 
to be standing on the beach of a Tuvaluan atoll (the small state comprises just 
nine separate low-lying islands, including six atolls). At the end of his speech, 
however, the camera slowly pans out to reveal that the minister is not standing 
on a real, physical island, but on a virtual, computer-animated one. This drama-
turgical trick visually supports the introduction of Te Ataeao Nei4  and the idea of 
a virtual nation.5  
The video, and the Te Ataeao Nei  / Future Now programme more broadly, 
can be seen as a partial embodiment of Tuvaluans’ resistance to their state being 
framed as an inevitable victim of global climate change. As Pacific scholars and 
others have argued, an imaginary of an inevitable victim rests at least partly on

German Research Foundation) under Germany’s Excellence Strategy EXC 2037 ‘CLICCS—Climate, climatic 
change, and society’, project  number 390683824, contribution to the Center for Earth System Research

Statehood in a world of environmental and technological change
The idea of a virtual state is not a new concept. 12 Examples range from rather 
modest initiatives for moving individual government institutions and services into 
virtual space to utopian visions for genuine cyber states. As early as the 2000s, 
different countries started operating in virtual environments. For example, in 
2006 the Maldives was the first country that opened an embassy in the virtual 
world of Second Life; others, including Sweden and Estonia, followed. 13  Second 
Life, a ‘metaverse before the metaverse’ according to Luciano Floridi, 14  was 
a virtual online world in which users could create their own avatars and travel 
between islands. In this setting, virtual embassies served mainly representative 
and economic functions—for example, attracting tourists and investors through 
online nation-branding.
Compared to earlier experiments with virtual embassies, the online repre-
sentation of Estonia was more complex. For example, it involved administrative 
services, including visa applications. It is often quoted as an example of a more 
ambitious vision of a ‘virtual state’.15  As part of its programme, which commenced 
in 2014, the Estonian government is handing out so-called ‘e-Residency’ or virtual

Virtual statehood in International Relations theory
Within IR, the political proposals and conceptual debates around the idea of 
deterritorial or virtual statehood described above tie in with ongoing discussions 
about changing forms of the state. The ideal-typical model of post-W estphalian 
statehood is enshrined in the 1933  Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties 
of States. 24  Article  1 of the Convention defines four essential qualifications of 
sovereign nation-states: a permanent population, a clearly defined territory, an 
independent government and the capacity to enter into relations with other states 
in the international system. After the end of the Cold War, in the context of 
globalization and digital transformation, this ideal-typical model of the nation-
state was perceived to be increasingly challenged. 25  The nation-state became 
more and more understood as historically contingent, rather than as a natural 
constant.26 In the dominant W estphalian model of the state, its sovereignty is 
linked to a physical territory with fixed, internationally recognized borders, home 
to a population defining itself as a nation. John Agnew was the most prominent 
critic of this ‘merging of the state with a clearly bounded territory’; he claimed 
that the discipline of IR was stuck in a ‘territorial trap’ 27 and that, under the 
influence of economic globalization and related transboundary flows of goods and 
‘bads’—from commodities to people, viruses or greenhouse gases—the ‘territo-
rial congruency between nation, state, society, and economy’ 28  was crumbling. 
Rather than being replaced by a new model of political authority, globalization 
scholars argued that the W estphalian state would become increasingly deterritorial-
ized. This process would involve the diffusion of authority below and above the 
national level in multilevel governance arrangements as well as the emergence 
of collective identities detached from territorial borders, for example in cyber -
space.29 Processes of (re)territorialization would simultaneously develop alongside

de jure and de facto understandings of sovereignty.33  While the former refers to the 
legal right of exercising coercive power over a defined territory based on interna-

The ‘trans-boundary character’ of current environmental anxieties (such as climate change 
in particular) not only disorients and dilates the notion of an unalloyed national territory 
but more pointedly announces the urgency for the ‘pooling’ of sovereignty itself ... In 
effect, engaging with environmental issues will require evolving common understand-
ings between states, who have to coordinate in concert rather than attempt a ‘drawbridge’ 
approach in which unilateral actions are carried out in the name of national security.35
To theorize this pooling of sovereignty, Agnew has proposed the notion of 
‘sovereignty regimes’.36  Such regimes refer to distributed spheres of political 
authority and allow one to conceive of central state authority in varying degrees, 
which ‘challenges the supposition that sovereignty is absolute and indivisible’.37

Performing statehood (through digital media)
While the discussed accounts of changing statehood are helpful in contextual-
izing and qualifying models of virtual states, they are limited in that they start 
from a single, western, notion of sovereignty. As stressed by anthropological and 
postcolonial scholarship, there are multiple ways in which the relation between 
territory and sovereignty can be articulated and practised. 39  By studying various 
processes of state formation empirically, such approaches have been able to show 
how any form of statehood relies on a whole variety of practices, discourses, 
symbols and tokens. 40  In short, this highlights the performative dimension of 
state formation and, importantly in our case, state preservation. Sovereign state-
hood is not fixed. Rather, it needs to be constantly re-enacted through national 
symbols, parades, architecture, diplomatic rituals and so on. In the age of social 
media and the internet, many of these state performances are mediated by digital 
technologies and media. 41  While some performances of sovereignty and state-
hood, such as diplomatic rituals, are often highly conventionalized, others are 
highly contextual, related to local, Indigenous customs, cultures and environ-
ments, thus bringing about a plurality of forms of statehood and ‘lived sover -
eignty’42  beyond the W estphalian model.43  In the context of islands, postcolonial

and adaptation in the context of sea-level rise. 47  Key to Tuvalu’s climate change

Considering this history, the Te Ataeao Nei  programme represents a critical 
juncture in Tuvalu’s climate policy. Though it remains committed to notions of 
self-determination and agency that have informed the country’s climate change 
strategy, it breaks with previous approaches by providing a defined worst-case 
strategy if Tuvalu’s territory becomes uninhabitable. In the past, such a scenario 
was acknowledged but not addressed in Tuvaluan climate policy. To retain self-
determination under conditions of extreme climate change, the Te Ataeao Nei  
programme51  involves three main strategies: the first initiative is the mainstreaming 
of key Tuvaluan values and norms in all the state’s diplomatic activities and inter-
national climate negotiations. It is hoped that notions such as fale pili (being a 
good neighbour) and kaitasi (shared responsibility) will encourage other nations to 
‘understand their shared responsibility to address international issues like climate 
change and sea level rise’.52  The second pillar of the programme is a diplomatic 
initiative to secure international recognition of Tuvalu’s statehood as permanent. 
Furthermore, along with a number of other (and larger) ocean states, Tuvalu is 
campaigning for an amendment to the 1982 UNCLOS that stipulates that states 
will not lose their right to their designated exclusive economic zones (EEZs) due 
to climate change and rising sea levels.53  W orking towards this reform, the govern-
ment insists that all countries forming relations with Tuvalu recognize the state-
hood of the nation as permanent and its existing maritime boundaries as set.54  The 
third pillar of the Te Ataeao Nei  programme is the proposal for building a virtual 
Tuvalu. This would involve ‘digitization activities on appropriate platforms 
to create a digital Government administrative system’. 55  Under a worst-case 
scenario, this would enable a future government to continue performing gover -
nance functions and providing services for a dispersed Tuvaluan people. Another 
important part of this strategy is the digitization of important political, cultural 
and historical documents, artefacts and practices to preserve them in the event of 
territorial loss.

in the face of ecological threats. The proposal attempts to answer an open question 
in Burkett’s concept of the ex-situ state: namely, where the government of such a 
state would be located. If we conceive of the government as a virtual government 
providing digital services to a ‘non-territorially bound imagined community’ of 
Tuvaluans, this question starts to be answered. 60  Another point is central from 
Tuvalu’s perspective: the spatial computing technologies behind the development 
of the metaverse would make it possible to link virtual space with physical space. 
On the project homepage, for example, this is indicated by the GPS coordinates 
at the top of the screen. The proposal of a digital state is thus crucially linked to 
Tuvalu’s claim for fixing its EEZ independently from its future physical territory. 
Rather than a decoupling of statehood and territory, the proposal describes a 
complex process of de- and reterritorialization. While the Tuvaluan people and 
its government may become mobile, dispersed across the globe and extended 
across cyberspace, we see simultaneous attempts at reterritorializing ocean- and 
cyberspace, for instance linking the EEZ to a virtual version of Tuvalu in the 
metaverse.
A contested proposal
Since Kofe’s video presentation at COP27, the Tuvalu government’s proposal has 
received much attention, meeting with some criticism from political and public 
commentators, including in Tuvalu itself. For example, on 31 May 2023 the leader 
of the opposition group in the Tuvaluan parliament released a media statement 
stating that:
The concept for the creation of a digital nation of Tuvalu in the metaverse implies that 
Tuvalu will disappear because of sea level rise and that we should make a digital copy of it. 
There is no basis of such proposition in international law, and there is absolutely no reason 
to believe that Tuvalu will disappear even with sea level rise.61
In support of that statement, Maina Talia, a climate action advocate, scholar and 
former director of the Tuvalu Association of NGOs,62 expressed similar concerns:
W e should not send a signal to the international community that it’s okay if Tuvalu 
drowns, if Tuvalu submerges, because they can always go to New Zealand or Australia 
… I’m not sure how it’s possible to go into another country and practice our own culture. 
That is impossible. Saving Tuvalu is literally saving our culture, saving our land, saving 
our people.63

digital country would be. In the early days of the internet, cyberspace was often 
envisioned as a new anarchic space that would eventually ‘replace the traditional 
territorial order of states’.69 Today, many authors paint a more complex picture 
of the changing nature of sovereignty and territory in cyberspace. For example, 
authors point to new forms of sovereignty emerging in virtual space, exercised 
by powerful digital platforms such as Meta, Google or Amazon. 70  In the age of 
platform capitalism, the internet has emerged as an asymmetrical space in which a 
few platforms have become the necessary passage points of global flows. 71 At the 
same time, states such as the United States or China, as well as supranational bodies 
like the European Union, are trying to regain sovereignty in virtual space through 
regulations, control mechanisms or national firewalls. The result is a complex 
landscape of overlapping sovereignty regimes, which is dominated by a few digital 
superpowers like the US and China and the big tech businesses operating on their 
territories or within their national economies. Uploading crucial government 
services or cultural resources to the cloud would create whole new dependencies 
on transnational corporations and IT infrastructures in other countries.
Towards a digital fenua
W e deem it important to consider these points of criticism and caveats related 
to platform capitalism and the metaverse when discussing the digital Tuvalu 
proposal. At the same time, it is important to stress that Tuvalu and other Pacific 
islands are actors in larger economic and geopolitical structures. While the idea 
of a virtual state has been articulated by big tech companies, western libertar -
ians and neo-liberal governments (as in the case of Estonia), such actors are not 
forcing this model upon the Tuvaluan government. Rather, the latter actively 
appropriates and rearticulates such imaginaries in relation to its demands, visions 
and traditions. Syncretism has a long tradition in the Pacific region, where local 
populations have historically succeeded in merging Indigenous cosmologies with 
western modernist institutions, such as territorial statehood. 72 With a view to 
Pacific climate discourses and the appropriation of western scientific concepts, 
Crook and Rudiak-Gould observe how Pacific peoples demonstrate an ‘adept skill 
in accepting external interests and turning them into home-grown initiatives’.73
